description: Houston-based team led by a USAMO qualifier and Codeforces Candidate Master with research experience in ML, optimization, and dynamical systems. We want to ship a working tool built on NASA open data by Sunday. Looking for teammates strong in web or front-end development, data visualization, graphic design, or presenting and storytelling. Beginners who can commit to both days are welcome. Message us with your skills and the challenge that interests you most.
summary: Signal or Noise? is a web tool that teaches students to test whether a change in NASA Earth data is real or random. Users pick a place and a variable from NASA GISTEMP, GPCP and NASA POWER, and the tool runs the Mann-Kendall test and Sen's slope, corrected for year-to-year memory. Every verdict comes with an uncertainty wedge and three detective checks: does one year decide it, did the pace change, and does a second test agree. A guided tour, four case files and a Noise Lab show how scientists reason. Findings include: 85% of Earth's surface warmed significantly since 1950, and the warming sped up after 1988; rainfall shifted while the global total held steady; and Houston's drying trend hinges on one hurricane year.
details:
What it does. Signal or Noise? is a single web page that lets anyone ask whether an Earth system variable is really changing. Users choose where to look (a world map of temperature or rainfall, or one of 42 places), what to look at (12 NASA POWER variables), and which season. The tool returns a trend, a verdict in plain English, and the evidence behind it. A guided tour walks a first-time user through eight steps using live numbers.

How it works. Each trend is measured with Sen's slope and tested with the Mann-Kendall test. The test is corrected for year-to-year memory using the Yue and Wang (2004) effective sample size, because climate records carry memory from one year to the next and an uncorrected test raises false alarms. A least-squares t-test with the same correction gives a second opinion. On the maps, a false discovery rate check (Benjamini and Hochberg 1995; Wilks 2016) keeps chance hits out when thousands of squares are tested at once.

Detective checks. Every verdict then faces three checks. A leave-one-year-out test shows whether a single year decides the result. A comparison of the two halves of the record tests whether the trend sped up, slowed or reversed. A moving-window chart shows how the trend changed over time. Every chart shades the 95% range of trend lines, so a student can see why a result is or is not significant.

We tested our own test. On thousands of simulated records with no trend, the Hamed-Rao correction we first used raised false alarms 17 to 28% of the time. We switched to a correction that gives about 5 to 7% for records of 50 years or more. Students can rerun this experiment in the Noise Lab, which also estimates how many years a trend needs before a test can catch it.

Key findings. From 1950 to 2025, 85% of Earth's surface warmed significantly, and the rate rose from 0.08 to 0.23 °C per decade between the two halves of the record (p = 0.0001). The Arctic has warmed 3.3 times as fast as the globe since 1980. Global rainfall barely changed (p = 0.79), yet 10% of the surface got wetter and 9% got drier. Relative humidity fell in Phoenix and rose in Delhi, both significantly. Houston rainfall trends down but is not yet significant (p = 0.10); removing 2017, the Hurricane Harvey year, alone would make it significant, and the Noise Lab estimates about 70 years of data are needed to confirm a trend that size.

Benefits and goals. The tool teaches the habit the challenge asks for: question a trend before trusting it. "Not significant" is presented as "not enough data yet" rather than "no change," and every claim shows its evidence. The goal is a classroom tool for high school Earth science and statistics.

Tools. The tool is one self-contained page (HTML, CSS and JavaScript) with no server. All tests run in the browser, in about half a second for a full map. Data were prepared in Python (NumPy, pandas, xarray) and embedded in compressed form. Charts on this page were plotted with matplotlib. The statistics were checked against pymannkendall, SciPy and an independent Python version on 85 series; p-values agree to within 0.0000001.

Methods references. Mann (1945); Kendall (1975); Sen (1968); Gilbert (1987); Hamed and Rao (1998); Yue and Wang (2004); Weatherhead et al. (1998); Benjamini and Hochberg (1995); Wilks (2016); Lenssen et al. (2019) for GISTEMP; Adler et al. (2018) for GPCP; Gelaro et al. (2017) for MERRA-2.

AI disclosure. Code, analysis, charts and text were developed with Claude (Anthropic), an AI assistant. The tool's footer, the final slide and the images below carry this disclosure.
